related_questions.question: How accurate are COVID PCR tests?

text_blocks.snippet: PCR tests for COVID-19 are highly accurate, with analytical performance approaching 100% in detecting the virus at high concentrations. However, clinical performance is influenced by factors like the timing of the test and how the sample is collected, and may be closer to 80% sensitivity and 98-99% specificity. PCR tests are considered more reliable than rapid antigen tests because they detect the virus's genetic material, minimizing interference from other viruses.

list.title: Analytical Sensitivity and Specificity:
list.snippet: PCR tests have high analytical sensitivity (ability to detect low viral loads) and specificity (ability to correctly identify negative samples).

list.title: Clinical Sensitivity:
list.snippet: Clinical sensitivity (the ability to correctly identify infected individuals) can be lower due to factors like timing of the test in relation to the infection cycle and the quality of the sample collection.

list.title: Timing of Testing:
list.snippet: PCR tests are most accurate when performed during the peak of infection when viral loads are highest, according to the College of American Pathologists. If symptoms are present but the initial PCR test is negative, retesting may be necessary.

list.title: Sample Collection:
list.snippet: Proper sample collection techniques are crucial for accurate results.

list.title: Interference:
list.snippet: While PCR tests are designed to minimize interference, other viruses can still potentially influence results in rare cases.

related_questions.question: Can a PCR test be wrong?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, PCR tests, including those for COVID-19, can be wrong. While generally accurate, PCR tests can produce false positive or false negative results.
snippet_highlighted_words: Yes, PCR tests, including those for COVID-19, can be wrong

text_blocks.snippet: A false positive means the test indicates you have the virus when you don't. This is more likely in low prevalence settings or with asymptomatic individuals without known exposure, according to the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

A false negative means the test doesn't detect the virus even though you are infected. This can happen due to various factors like timing of the test, the quality of the sample, or the test's sensitivity.
